newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Greenpeace blames US for failed climate talks.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace blames US for failed climate talks.

text.p: Environmental activists, including Greenpeace International and the World Wide Fund for Nature, blamed the United States and France on Friday for what they called failed negotiations on cutting greenhouse gas emissions.
But conference officials, who admitted that industrialised countries had clashed over their future commitments to protect the climate, put on a brave face after the week-long talks.
The ultimate objective was reaching a global accord at a ministerial summit in Kyoto, Japan in December 1997, they said.
Greenhouse gas emissions including carbon dioxide (CO2) are blamed by scientists for global warming, a phenomenon which adversely affects human health as well as food and water supplies.
Officials from some 140 countries which have ratified the 1992 Climate Change Convention, signed at the Rio Earth Summit to stabilise concentrations of greenhouse gases, took part.

They were debating timetables and targets in a future treaty protocol which would commit industrialised countries to cut their greenhouse-gas emissions after the year 2000. Developing countries are exempted but may be asked to make voluntary cuts.
Delegates gave the chairman a mandate to incorporate various positions into a text to be negotiated at the next round of talks in February in Bonn.
Environmentalist groups charged major countries had played into the hands of the fossil fuel (coal and oil) industry.
"The U.S. has obstructed progress all the way through this meeting by rejecting early action to cut CO2 emissions," said Bill Hare, climate policy director at Greenpeace International.
"Japan and the U.S. are playing right into the hands of the fossil fuel industry by allowing the core issue -- binding CO2 cuts, start now -- to be obscured," he said in a statement.
The World Wide Fund for Nature, based in Gland, Switzerland, issued a separate statement headlined "A Wasted Week".
"The United States managed to throw major obstacles into the negotiations this week and have tried to reopen previous agreements," the WWF said.
"The only new idea they added was to try to borrow emission rights from future generations."

Both environmental groups said it was essential to start discussing a concrete proposal at the next meeting in Bonn, which will be followed by August and October sessions in the German city leading up to the summit in Japan.
Conference officials were defensive.
"I don't think you can call a negotiation a failure before it is over," Michael Zammit Cutajar, executive secretary of the Convention, told a final news conference.
"What clearly gives rise to concern is how far apart countries are still, sometimes on very fundamental points. It is useless expecting big advances at this point," he added.

Some governments argued for 10 percent reductions in carbon dioxide (CO2) by the year 2005. Some called for 20 percent cuts by then, while others found the timetable unrealistic and proposed a 10 percent cut by the year 2010, officials said.
Some governments called for "flexible policies" with measures adapted to national circumstances, while others backed "differentiated commitments" based on per capita targets.
John Grasser, of the National Mining Association in Washington, D.C., defended industry interests and criticised some tough targets under consideration.
"The U.S. Congress would never support these targets. They would impair economic growth. The sky isn't falling yet, there's time to do analysis so we can get it right," he told Reuters.

"An unfair process would simply wipe out Australia's coal and aluminium industries," added John Hannagan, of Australian Business Council. Some 15 per cent of Australia's export revenues come from coal, he said. REUTER
